In analyzing the socio-economic impacts, it is extremely important to consider the various levels and rates of coal mining. A rapid rate of development and early achievement of high levels of production will severely test any rural area's service and supply sectors as the limitations of the local labor force induce heavy migration of construction workers into the growth area. Similarly, rapid population increases, associated with high levels of net in-migration may place severe stress on the existing social and institutional systems as well as the present services. Although there will be obvious economic benefits resulting from the employment, the rapid changes in population may create social conflict and division in the community, unless appropriate plans are made and steps taken to forestall such events.
In reporting the impact analysis, the most probable scenario (low level) will receive most emphasis since it is required by an existing lease agreement specifying production levels and time schedules.
In attempting to isolate the impact of the Westmoreland Resources lease development, it is important to remember that the lease tracts cannot be considered a "developmental island". Very extensive coal development, possibly including synfuel conversion (gasification) plants, will be taking place in areas in the vicinity of the Ceded Area. These adjacent developments will be competing for labor, housing, goods and services, and other facilities. In order to consider Westmoreland Resources development in light of other mining activities involving Crow coal resources, two different "Alternative Futures" were used in the analytical model as bases from which to measure Westmoreland Resources' impact.
